rows.04:095c:
...Still, I can't believe you're going on with this.
{a}, was it?
You've got some real guts, you know that?
Well?{p}Don't you actually want to quit already?
rows.04:0a30:
Still, it's gotten pretty lonely in here.
There were six of us at the start, and now we're down to three.
And the last one who's supposed to tell a story still hasn't shown up.
Well, I guess that doesn't matter.
No point making a fuss about it now.{p}
rows.04:0b34:
Well then, let me introduce myself.
My name's Makoto Shindo.
I'm a third-year.
Good to meet you.{p}
rows.04:0b94:
You know our school's got a whole pile of sports clubs that are regulars at the national tournament, right?
Baseball and soccer.
Judo and kendo.
Tennis and table tennis.
Well, we've got plenty of talent here.
Which means the teams run deep.
Anyway, among all those sports clubs, there was one that set just as many brilliant records as the ones I just named.
Though it's gone completely to seed these days.
Can you guess which one?{p}
rows.04:0d2c:
...It's the boxing club.
Boxing's great.
It's a man's sport.
It's the kind of sport a woman can't really understand, right?
People who don't get boxing say it's just a slugfest, just a brawl, but that's dead wrong.
You'd be hard pressed to find a more gentlemanly sport anywhere, don't you think?
Our school's boxing club was really something back in the day, too.
It showed up at the nationals pretty much every single year.
And it placed near the top in a whole bunch of weight classes.
Impressive, huh?{p}
rows.04:0f10:
But now it's no good.
No good at all.
The membership's dropped way off, too.
There's not a trace left of what it used to be.
It's turned into a ghost club, clinging to its past glory and only still around out of pity.
But there's a little reason behind that.
The scary story I'm going to tell you is about that boxing club.{p}
rows.04:1044:
The boxing club didn't just get strong on its own.
And it's not like only guys with talent sign up, either.
In sports, guts count for more than talent.
The boxing club got strong by beating those guts into shape.
That's what they call hard training.
It's not bullying, mind you.
It's training.{p}
rows.04:1160: Our boxing club had a traditional kind of training that got handed down from one generation to the next.{p}You know what kind of training it was?
rows.04:121c:
That's right, the one they also call the Hell Camp.
When summer vacation comes, they hole up in the mountains for three whole weeks.
Of course, there's brutal training before that, too.
Hard training from the alumni, three round trips running to the shrine.{p}
rows.04:1350:
At the start, there are about forty new members.
The tough training cuts that down to about half.
And then comes the summer Hell Camp.
The twenty or so who somehow made it that far get whittled down to five at this camp.
Surprised, huh?
But those five are strong, let me tell you.
After all, they're the five who survived the Hell Camp.
Their guts are on a whole other level.
They're the ones who carry the boxing club's tradition and pass it on.{p}...So, do you want to know what goes on at that camp?
rows.04:14f8:
Heh heh... So you want to know, huh?
You're really into this stuff, aren't you?
You just love cruel stories, is that it?
Or are you the type who loves other people's misery?
Well, whatever.
Then I'll tell you.{p}
rows.04:15bc:
In the morning, they get up at four, chop firewood and do morning practice.
Then they make breakfast.
After they eat, it's weight training and running the mountain trails.
That's rough, let me tell you.{p}
rows.04:1654:
Then they make lunch.
The first-years do all the cooking, see.
And if it tastes bad, they get punched out.
On top of that, three hundred push-ups.
Just because the food tasted bad.
That's torture, isn't it?
But that's just the beginning.
If that was all, it wouldn't be bad enough to be called the Hell Camp.{p}
rows.04:1770:
The real trouble is the afternoon.
In the afternoon, the first-years, one at a time, spar against every single senior.
Three rounds with each one.
There are only about ten seniors, but they're guys who place near the top at the nationals.
You get made to fight those guys for thirty rounds total.
It's nothing but torture.
It's 'training' in name only. Frankly, it's bullying.{p}
rows.04:189c:
Well, hardly anybody lasts to the end.
They usually end up passing out partway through.
Even when they pass out, they get water dumped on them and get hauled back to their feet.
And then they're made to keep fighting.
A living punching bag.
A leather sack stuffed with flesh and blood instead of sand.
In a single day, the first-years' faces swell up like balloons. It's a parade of monsters.{p}
rows.04:19f4:
And guys like that are crawling all over, deep in the mountains.
If some hiker happened to stumble across them...
Maybe that's what ghosts really are, huh?
Ah ha ha ha...
...Well, let's keep going.{p}
rows.04:1ad8:
So anyway, they keep up that training, or torture, or bullying, whatever you want to call it, right?
Within three days, most of the guys have run off, just like that.
They sneak away in the middle of the night.
And in the end, they're down to about five.
Let's see, how many years ago was it?
I think it was about fifteen years ago.
That year, the Hell Camp was held just like every other year.
Twenty-three first-years took part in the camp.
They'd all heard the rumors about the camp, see.
Most of them were nervous wrecks, but a few of them were calm.
They were sure of themselves, saying they'd be fine.
Though it's always guys like that who end up being the first to run off.{p}
rows.04:1d3c: Now, among the first-years that year was a guy named Yosuke Akasaka.
rows.04:1d6c:
You couldn't really call him the sturdy type.
But he loved boxing.
He idolized strong boxers.
He looked like the type who gets picked on, Akasaka did.
Honestly, the seniors figured he'd be the very first to quit.
But it turned out he had guts.
Say what you will, he lasted all the way to the camp.
Still, everyone was sure he'd have quit by the time the camp was over.
And with that in mind, they zeroed in on Akasaka as their target.
The target of their training.{p}
rows.04:1f40:
Frankly, call it training or drills or whatever, I think for the seniors it was also a way to blow off steam and work off stress.
On the surface, they said all the right things, about honoring tradition and building mental toughness that way.
But in reality, it was nothing of the sort.
It really was just bullying.{p}
rows.04:21cc: And they decided to ask Akasaka to come along.{p}What do you think Akasaka said?
rows.04:2220: I'll stick it out to the end
rows.04:2234: I'll tell the seniors on you!
rows.04:225c:
Akasaka had guts.
No matter how hard they tried to talk him into it, he wouldn't run.
He insisted he'd see the camp through to the end.
But here's the thing.
Once he said that, the first-years who'd suggested the escape suddenly got worried.
They'd been sure Akasaka would go along with it, see.
That's why they'd asked him.
But he flatly refused.
And that made them nervous.{p}
rows.04:23d4:
Akasaka was sure to report this to the seniors.
Then they'd be the ones on the receiving end of the training.
It was hard enough already. If they got any more, they'd really die.
They all started shaking like leaves.
Then they crowded in on Akasaka.
"Hey.
You keep this a secret, got it?"
"...Yeah, I won't tell."
But none of them believed what Akasaka said.
Even if they wanted to believe him, they were worried sick.{p}
rows.04:2574:
So they called him out.
While they were making dinner, they ganged up on Akasaka and beat him.
Pretty awful, huh?
They all had a lot of pent-up frustration, see.
At first, they only meant to rough him up a little.
But it didn't stop there.
It kept escalating.
Maybe Akasaka was just the kind of guy who gets picked on by nature.
All of them, like they were possessed by something, punched Akasaka and kicked him.{p}
rows.04:26f4:
"I'm borrowing your gloves."
The ringleader was a guy named Toru Hatanaka.
He took Akasaka's gloves and pounded on Akasaka like he was a real punching bag.
"S-stop it... What did I ever do to you?"
"Heh.
You haven't done anything yet, so we're taking care of it now, while we can.
If we leave you alone, you'll rat on us for sure.
Listen, don't you dare rat to the seniors that we tried to run away."
And with that, he punched Akasaka over and over and over again.{p}
rows.04:28a0:
"Got it?!
Don't you dare rat on us!"
"......"
Akasaka didn't answer any more after that.
"Hey, Toru.
That's enough.
He's out cold."
If one of them hadn't stopped him, Hatanaka would have kept on beating Akasaka.{p}
rows.04:2978:
The gloves were smeared with blood.
Boxing gloves are red to begin with, right?
When they get blood on them, see, those worn-out old gloves shine and gleam like they're brand new.
"Here, you can have them back."{p}
rows.04:2a38: He flung the gloves down, smashing them into Akasaka's face as he lay there limp.{p}
rows.04:2aa4:
Then they all went back to making dinner.
They left Akasaka there, all alone.
"Hey! Where's Akasaka?"
Even at mealtime, Akasaka didn't show up.
Then again, it was normal for some of the first-years to feel too sick to eat.
So they could easily fool the seniors when they asked.
"Akasaka said he wasn't feeling well, so he's lying down, sir!"
The seniors didn't press any further.
After they'd cleared away the meal, Hatanaka and the others hurried to the spot where they'd beaten Akasaka.{p}
rows.04:2c5c:
Akasaka was still there.
Lying limp, just the way they'd left him.
"Hey, Akasaka!
Quit fooling around and get up."
Hatanaka gave Akasaka a light kick in the stomach.
But something was off.
It was like kicking a lump of soft rubber. He didn't react at all.
Not the way a living person would.{p}
rows.04:2d64:
"...Hey, Toru!
He's dead!"
The guy who'd tried to help Akasaka up couldn't help shouting.
"...You're kidding, right?"
Hatanaka didn't believe it.
He never imagined a guy who'd held up under all that training would die from a little roughing up.
But he was dead.
No matter how they called his name, no matter how they shook him, he didn't so much as twitch.
He wasn't breathing.
"...What do we do, Toru?
We're screwed."
The guys who'd beaten Akasaka along with him sounded like they were about to die themselves.
Well, of course they did.
They'd killed someone.
And they'd all ganged up on him to do it...{p}So, what do you think they did?
rows.04:2fcc:
"L-let's bury him."
Hatanaka muttered it under his breath, with a ghastly look on his face.
Everyone looked at Hatanaka's face, worried.
But maybe there really was no other way.{p}
rows.04:307c:
That night, after everyone was asleep, they buried Akasaka's body.
In secret.
Running away was the last thing on their minds now.
"Where'd Akasaka go?!"
Even when the seniors yelled, they all just put on innocent faces and cocked their heads.
"...He looked like he was having a hard time.
Maybe he ran off?"
And that satisfied everybody.
He'd been on the list of likely dropouts from the start, after all.
Some of the seniors even nodded like they were glad.
Pretty smug of them, huh?{p}
rows.04:323c:
As for Hatanaka and the others, they spent the rest of the camp jumpy and scared that they'd be found out.
Maybe that was a blessing, because Hatanaka and his bunch made it through the Hell Camp.
Turn misfortune into a blessing... is that how the saying goes?
It was just like that saying.{p}
rows.04:3328:
Once you make it through the camp, you're a full-fledged member.
First-years who'd been treated like bugs until then finally get recognized as human beings.
And they gain confidence, too.
So they get stronger fast.
Say what you want, that camp really does work.
But the Akasaka business did turn into a problem.
Even if he'd run away from camp, he never made it back home.{p}
rows.04:346c:
A search party went out.
But they didn't find him.
Hatanaka and the others were scared out of their minds about what would happen if the body turned up.
Even so, nothing was found, and the search was called off.
After that, Hatanaka and the rest were back to their smug selves.
They forgot all about Akasaka in no time.
...And then a year went by.{p}
rows.04:3590:
Hatanaka and the others were second-years now.
This time, it was their turn to put the first-years through the training.
They went at it brutally, like they were paying back everything they'd been through.
Now that it was their turn, it really hit them how much fun dishing out the training could be.
The club that had been so painful until then turned rosy overnight.
Then the annual summer camp drew near.
But along with it, the memory of Akasaka came back to them.{p}
rows.04:3708:
Going to camp meant going to that place.
They'd have to go to the place where Akasaka was buried.
"What do we do, Toru?
Are you going to the camp?"
The guys who'd been in on it back then all looked uneasy.{p}
rows.04:37c4: Well?{p}Do you think Hatanaka went to the camp?

notes: 04:0a30: 'six of us ... down to three' assumes Shindo is the third storyteller of this run (route-dependent order).
04:2234: choice 'I'll tell the seniors on you!' compresses 'if you say that I'll tell on you to the seniors' to fit one line.
